issues.legal_issue: A Union law declaring Union control over mineral conservation and development supersedes State legislation to the extent that both cover the same field.
material_facts: The State law authorized a levy on minerals extracted in designated mining areas, with the proceeds used for amenities and development in those areas.
The later Union law declared Union control over the regulation of mines and development of minerals and imposed a duty to take all necessary steps for their conservation and development.
The Court found no material difference between the relevant scope of the earlier Union law considered in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa and the later Union law.
issues.conclusion: The Union law covered the field occupied by the State law, so the State law was superseded to that extent and the State lacked legislative competence over that field.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 246 and the distribution of legislative subjects in the Seventh Schedule, State legislative power over mines and mineral development is subject to Union legislation under Entry 54 of List I. A parliamentary declaration taking control of a field removes that field from Entry 23 of List II to the declared extent. Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa was followed: the declaration and legislation covering the field, rather than any conflict between particular provisions, determine whether State competence is displaced.

rule.if: competing_legislation_case and union_control_declaration_made and union_law_covers_same_field and state_law_relates_to_that_field

predicates.competing_legislation_case: The case concerns legislation by different levels of government addressing an overlapping subject.
predicates.union_control_declaration_made: The Union legislature declared that Union control over a subject was expedient in the public interest.
predicates.union_law_covers_same_field: The Union law covers the field addressed by the State law.
predicates.state_law_relates_to_that_field: The State law regulates or imposes a levy in relation to that same field.

issues.definition: When competing legislation involves a Union declaration and a Union law covering the field addressed by a State law, the State law is superseded within that field.

issues.legal_issue: A Union law that manifests an intention to cover an entire field can displace State legislation even before rules are made under the Union law.
material_facts: The Union law imposed a duty to take all necessary steps for mineral conservation and development and authorized rules for that purpose.
No rules had been made that imposed the same levy or provided the same amenities as the State law.
The Court found that the Union law manifested an intention to cover the entire field of mineral development.
issues.conclusion: The absence of implementing rules did not prevent the Union law from displacing the State law in the field it covered.
issues.legal_principle: Repugnancy is not confined to contradictory provisions. Where legislation of superior efficacy manifests an intention to cover the whole field, legislation by the other legislature is displaced even without a detailed comparison of provisions. The Court relied on Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa for the proposition that the parliamentary declaration need not be followed by rules for the field to be taken over. Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh was distinguished because the present law manifested an intention to occupy the entire field.

predicates.competing_legislation_case: The case concerns legislation by different levels of government addressing an overlapping subject.
predicates.union_law_manifests_intent_to_cover_enti: The Union law expresses an intention to regulate the whole relevant field.
predicates.implementing_rules_not_made: No rules implementing the Union law in the overlapping area had been made.

issues.definition: Where a Union law manifests an intention to cover the entire field, State legislation in that field is displaced even if implementing rules have not been made.

issues.legal_issue: A State cannot impose a fee in respect of a subject that has been removed from its legislative field by Union control.
material_facts: The State imposed a fee on minerals extracted from mining areas to fund development and amenities there.
The Court held that the Union law had taken over the field of mineral conservation and development, leaving no part of that subject within the relevant State legislative field.
The State argued that the power to impose fees was an independent legislative head.
issues.conclusion: The State fee could not be sustained after the subject to which it related had been taken over by the Union.
issues.legal_principle: Although the legislative lists separately provide for the power to impose fees, a fee must be in respect of a matter within the legislature’s field. Article 246 and the relevant Union and State list entries leave no State matter to support a fee where Union control has removed the underlying subject from the State field.

predicates.fee_validity_case: The case concerns whether a government may impose a fee.
predicates.state_fee_relates_to_union_controlled_su: The State imposed a fee in respect of a subject controlled by the Union.
predicates.subject_removed_from_state_field: The relevant subject had been removed from the State legislature’s field.

issues.definition: A State fee is not valid when it relates to a subject controlled by the Union and removed from the State legislature’s field.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory saving for repeal preserves liabilities that accrued before an implied repeal or supersession unless the later law shows a contrary intention.
material_facts: The liabilities for fees accrued under the State law before the Union law displaced it.
The State served demands for those accrued fees after the displacement.
The Court found no contrary intention in the later law that would extinguish the accrued liabilities.
The State appealed from a judgment that had set aside the demands and sought to enforce the accrued liabilities.
issues.conclusion: The accrued liabilities remained enforceable, so the demands for the pre-supersession fees were valid and the appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 preserves accrued rights and liabilities when an enactment is repealed unless a different intention appears. The Court held that this principle applies to implied as well as express repeal: the form of repeal does not change the legislative intention to supersede the earlier law. Kay v. Goodwin and Surtees v. Ellison were cited for the general effect of repeal absent a saving; Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay and Trust Mai Lachhmi Sialkoti Bradari v. Chairman, Amritsar Improvement Trust were considered, but did not determine the question in a way that displaced this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_from_judgment_setting_aside_demand and liability_accrued_under_valid_law_before_supersession and later_law_superseded_that_law and no_contrary_intention_to_erase_liability and demand_seeks_enforcement_of_accrued_liability

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_setting_aside_deman: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment that set aside a demand seeking payment of a liability.
predicates.liability_accrued_under_valid_law_before: The liability accrued under a law that was valid before that law was superseded.
predicates.later_law_superseded_that_law: A later law superseded the earlier law.
predicates.no_contrary_intention_to_erase_liability: The later law did not show an intention to extinguish liabilities already accrued under the earlier law.
predicates.demand_seeks_enforcement_of_accrued_liab: The demand seeks payment of a liability that accrued before the earlier law was superseded.

issues.definition: When a demand in an appeal seeks enforcement of a liability accrued under a valid law before supersession, and the later law does not show an intention to erase it, the liability remains enforceable.
